soil-bio-026.title: Three ways to draw who eats whom in soil
soil-bio-026.text: In 1912, a food web traced the predators and parasites of the cotton boll weevil. It was the first topological web, the earliest of three ways to draw a food web. Topological webs map which organisms eat which, without numbers. Flow webs add numbers to the links, as {{ref:soil-bio-027}} shows. Interaction webs show how one group influences another. Each link has a positive effect on the consumer and a negative one on the resource, and these links can cause indirect effects. Community matrix models describe every link with differential equations. They use Lotka–Volterra equations and data on biomass and feeding rate to calculate interaction strengths. Comparisons stay difficult, because authors lump different numbers of species into functional groups.

soil-bio-027.title: Flow webs put numbers on soil's feeding links
soil-bio-027.text: In 1987, Hunt and colleagues put numbers on a soil food web for the first time. Their flow web covered the shortgrass prairie of Colorado. It estimated how much nitrogen passed between soil organisms and how fast each released it in mineral form. A flow web traces how much carbon or other nutrients move from producers to consumers. Building one starts from a topological web. Each functional group's biomass is then calculated, usually in kg carbon/hectare. Assuming populations are at equilibrium lets researchers derive feeding rates. Flow webs revealed three main energy channels. The bacterial and fungal channels carry the largest flow, the root-herbivory channel much less. Bacteria and fungi are now widely recognized as critical to decomposing carbon and nitrogen.

soil-bio-007.title: Does life underground follow the map of life above?
soil-bio-007.text: Does life underground follow the same map as life above it? Studies disagree, and the question is open. A survey of 17,516 18S rRNA gene sequences from 20 phyla of soil animals hinted that below-ground animal diversity may run opposite to above-ground diversity. Soil biodiversity lacks the clear latitudinal gradients, the shifts with distance from the equator, seen in plants. In 2007, salinity, not temperature or pH, was found to be the main global determinant of bacterial diversity. A 2014 global study found fungal richness unrelated to plant diversity and better explained by climate, then soil and spatial factors. The stakes are disputed too. Some studies find that losing soil organisms reduces many ecosystem functions; others find plant diversity a better predictor.

soil-bio-006.title: Microbial hotspots, the crowded corners of soil
soil-bio-006.text: Soil microbes do not spread evenly. They crowd into hotspots, small sites rich in resources such as moisture or nutrients. One is the soil around roots. Another is the detritusphere, where dead organic material accumulates. In both, decaying root litter and compounds released by roots regulate the supply of carbon and nitrogen and so steer microbial processes. Root tips are hotspots of cellulase and chitinase, enzymes that break down plant and fungal materials. Between hotspots, microbes are separated in space. That separation, shaped by easily used carbon, temperature and moisture, affects how they interact and how the soil ecosystem works.

soil-bio-061.title: Living on almost nothing in deep and frozen soils
soil-bio-061.text: In farmed and frozen soils, microbes live on very little. These oligotrophic soil environments are home to the specialists described in {{ref:soil-bio-060}}. Nutrients thin out with depth. Surface microbes quickly consume what decomposes from plant and animal debris, and their wastes build up toxic chemicals lower down. Water and oxygen also diffuse less easily as depth increases. Aggregates, pores and extracellular enzymes help water, oxygen and nutrients move into the soil. Frozen polar soils are dominated by Actinomycetota, Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Cyanobacteria. Actinomycetota keep their enzymes working across a wide range of low temperatures. The bacterium Collimonas survives by digesting chitin from fungi and by weathering rocks and minerals for electron sources.

soil-bio-062.title: How plants thrive on the poorest soils
soil-bio-062.text: Plants on nutrient-poor soils get by in three ways: they take up nutrients more efficiently, use less of them and store them. Root adaptations improve uptake, among them nitrogen-fixing root nodules, fungal partners and cluster roots. These plants grow very slowly. They use abundant ions to keep their cells firm and save scarce nutrients for building tissue. Many store nutrients, in trunk tissue for example, and remobilize them when demand rises. On the ancient sandplains of southern Western Australia, most plants rely on cluster roots for phosphorus and sulfur. Yet the vegetation is highly diverse. The white-sand soils of the Rio Negro basin in northern Amazonia, with pH below 5.0, tell another story. They carry low-diversity, extremely fragile forests and savannahs.

soil-bio-046.title: The drilosphere, soil remade by earthworms
soil-bio-046.text: Every earthworm burrow is wrapped in a lining of altered soil. The drilosphere is the part of the soil shaped by earthworm secretions, burrowing and casts: soil that has passed through their gut or lines their burrows. The lining averages 2 mm thick but can reach about 8 mm around the burrows of litter-feeding earthworms. It is generally richer in nitrogen, phosphorus and well-decayed organic material than the soil around it, probably because earthworms prefer to eat leaf and root litter. Microbes gather there too. In one soil it held 40 percent of the aerobic and 13 percent of the anaerobic nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and 16 percent of the denitrifiers. Through it, earthworms steer soil microbes and, with them, the fate of nutrients.

soil-bio-024.title: Moles, gophers and badgers: the giants that dig soil
soil-bio-024.text: Moles, pocket gophers, voles and badgers are the giants of soil life. Soil megafauna are soil animals over 2 cm long, mostly burrowing vertebrates that dig nests and galleries and throw earth up into mounds. Besides these digging mammals, they include burrowing birds, reptiles, amphibians, large earthworms and big arthropods. They are most common in arid areas. Most dig without eating soil. Still, stirring the horizons improves nutrient availability, infiltration, aeration, seed germination and the spread of fungi that partner with roots. Burrows create nutrient-rich patches and raise porosity and infiltration, reducing runoff on slopes. These animals are often treated as pests. Yet their loss from whole landscapes has been called an ecological catastrophe, especially in dry lands, where they are keystone species for healthy soil.

soil-bio-021.title: Soil microfauna, the animals that live in water films
soil-bio-021.text: A tardigrade dried out in soil can wait as a shrunken tun and revive within a few hours. Tardigrades belong to the soil microfauna, the smallest soil animals at 20 μm to 200 μm. The group includes protozoa, nematodes and rotifers. They move through mesopores (30–75 μm) and macropores (>75 μm) and mostly live in the water films around aggregates and roots. There they eat microbes or one another. Their grazing rejuvenates microbial colonies, and they excrete nutrients such as ammonium in a form plants can use. Tied to pore water, they are sensitive to drying. Cysts, dauer larvae and tuns are their survival stages. Unlike most soil invertebrates, they may not suffer critically from climate warming, but they are highly sensitive to acid rain.

soil-bio-083.title: Entomopathogenic nematodes, worms that hunt insects
soil-bio-083.text: Within 24–48 hours of a tiny worm getting inside, an insect is dead. Entomopathogenic nematodes are thread worms that infect and kill only insects, living as parasites inside them. Their targets live in the soil, from the larvae of moths, flies and beetles to adult grasshoppers and crickets. An infective juvenile enters an insect and releases gut bacteria, Xenorhabdus or Photorhabdus, that kill it. After about a week, hundreds of thousands of new juveniles leave the cadaver. Hunting styles differ. Ambushers such as Steinernema carpocapsae wait at the surface for surface insects. Cruisers such as Heterorhabditis bacteriophora hunt deeper, so {{ref:soil-agri-095}} cut the first's numbers but left the second's unchanged. Both groups are used in biological pest control. Together they cut plum curculio populations by as much as 70–90% in northeastern American orchards. They fail against foliage pests, because UV light and drying harm them.

soil-bio-088.title: Copiotrophs, the microbes that live for the feast
soil-bio-088.text: Some bacteria live for the feast. A copiotroph is an organism of nutrient-rich environments, especially rich in carbon, and the opposite of an oligotroph. Copiotrophs grow at organic substrate levels up to 100 times higher. They live a feast-and-famine life. Motile and chemotactic, they move toward chemical cues, rush to nutrients and use them fast. Once supplies run out they survive poorly, and oligotrophs outcompete them. Their genes are built for speed: they carry up to fifteen ribosomal RNA operons, against one in oligotrophs, but use carbon less efficiently. Soil bacterial phyla can be sorted into the two groups. Soils rich in organic carbon favor copiotrophs, key players in carbon cycling when plants exude simple compounds such as sugars.

soil-found-076.title: The fungal loop that links desert plants and crusts
soil-found-076.text: In dry lands, life wakes in pulses after rain, and fungi may keep the pulses connected. The fungal loop hypothesis proposes that soil fungi in arid ecosystems link plants with a {{ref:soil-phys-032}}, which responds to a different amount of moisture. Crusts wake after small rains. Fungi hold their nutrients until larger rains activate plants, which then pass carbon back to their fungal partners. Carbon and nutrients thus stay cycling in living pools instead of washing away or escaping to the air between rains. Fungi suit the job. They work at higher temperatures and in drier soil than bacteria, so they likely drive nutrient cycling in hot, dry ecosystems. Direct tests remain rare. One isotope study found nitrogen moving up to 100 cm per day in both directions between plants and crust.

soil-bio-053.title: Saprotrophic bacteria, which digest the dead from outside
soil-bio-053.text: Many soil bacteria digest their food before they eat it. Saprotrophic bacteria, mostly soil-dwelling, feed on dead organic material. They release enzymes that digest it outside the cell, then absorb the products. Alongside saprotrophic fungi and water molds, they drive the breakdown of dead matter and the cycling of nutrients, and they feed higher trophic levels. Bacteria outcompete fungi for easily available food. In forest soils, though, their higher nitrogen demand and inability to move nutrients make them less efficient at breaking litter down. Their community make-up and growth rates signal the soil's condition, since growth responds quickly to change. Some are pathogens spread through contact with excrement, such as Escherichia coli. Others ferment cellulose in the rumen of cows.

soil-bio-082.title: The Mendocino staircase, where old soil grows pygmy pines
soil-bio-082.text: On the northern California coast, a pine with 80 or more growth rings may stand barely three or four feet high. It grows on the Mendocino ecological staircase, a flight of uplifted marine terraces. Each terrace is about 100,000 years older than the one below and carries its own soils, microbes, plants and animals. Plant succession repeated on each terrace eventually forms a very acid, nutrient-poor soil, the Blacklock series, with a clay or iron hardpan beneath. These pygmy forest soils are low in macro- and micronutrients and high in exchangeable aluminum. The iron hardpan blocks deep roots and internal drainage. On younger soils nearby, the same pine species grows many dozens of feet high. {{ref:soil-hist-010}} studied the pygmy forest on a 500,000-year-old terrace. The staircase shows one soil passing through several successive steady states. In 1974 the site became the Pygmy Forest National Natural Landmark.

soil-bio-072.title: The order in which fungi follow a flood of ammonia
soil-bio-072.text: When ammonia or {{ref:soil-fert-021}} reaches forest soil, {{ref:soil-bio-071}} fruit in a set order as the pH falls. Anamorphic fungi come first, tolerating pH above 8. Once they bring the pH to 7, cup fungi (Ascomycota) develop, and at pH 6 small basidiomycetes follow. These early-phase fungi fruit 20 to 200 days after application, in alkaline to neutral soils rich in ammonium-nitrogen. They usually run only one cycle. Late-phase agarics, with larger fruiting bodies, develop once the pH is 3.5–6.0, typically 2–3 years after application. They gradually turn soil ammonium into nitrate-nitrogen. Late-phase fungi are larger and more numerous and can recur over several cycles. Most are biotrophic, living off living partners, and few feed on dead matter.

soil-bio-068.title: Biocementation: bacteria that keep sand from liquefying
soil-bio-068.text: In triaxial tests, bio-cemented Ottawa sand grew 1.8 times stronger in shear. Biocementation uses {{ref:soil-bio-067}} as a cementing technique to strengthen sand that might otherwise liquefy. Treated sand gains shear strength, compressive strength, stiffness and resistance to liquefaction, because grains are bonded and the soil becomes denser. Strength comes mostly from point-to-point contacts between carbonate crystals and sand grains. Trickling solution from the surface forms crystals at the bridges between grains, so it gives more strength per amount of calcite. The method could be a cheap, green alternative to chemical grouting, whose synthetic additives are costly and, except for sodium silicate, toxic. It has limits. Bacteria cannot pass pore throats smaller than about 0.4 μm, so it suits soils with few fines (USCS GW, GP, SW, SP, ML and organic soils). Enriching native urea-splitting bacteria in place can help.

soil-bio-055.title: The enzymatic latch that holds decay in check
soil-bio-055.text: In {{ref:soil-class-070}}, one family of enzymes holds the key to decay. The enzymatic latch is the control of breakdown in this waterlogged material by phenol oxidases. Phenolic compounds inhibit the hydrolase enzymes that digest dead material. Phenol oxidases destroy those phenolics and so release decay, which means limits on the microbes limit breakdown. Saprotrophic bacteria release microbial extracellular enzymes (MEEs) when their energy and nutrient needs are unmet, so MEEs signal nutrient availability. Several tell a story. β-glucosidase releases sugars that give microbes energy and easily used carbon. Acid and alkaline phosphatases show the potential to free phosphorus from organic forms. Phenol oxidases can also degrade or detoxify aromatic pollutants into carbon sources.

soil-bio-054.title: How fast soil bacteria grow and replace themselves
soil-bio-054.text: Next to young roots, a soil bacterial population can turn over in well under a day. Soil bacterial growth rate measures how fast bacteria produce new biomass and replace their populations. Under normal conditions production stays fairly steady, as growth is balanced by predation and other deaths. Estimates of turnover vary widely. Leucine or thymidine incorporation suggests days to weeks at around 20 °C. Other studies estimate 107–160 days at 25 °C, a gap put down to methods and temperature. The soil around roots is a special case. Compounds released by roots cut turnover there to 12–19 hours, shorter on younger roots. Growth rises with soil moisture. Added glucose boosts it at low concentrations but inhibits it at very high ones.

soil-bio-038.title: The Birch effect: a burst of breath when rain hits dry soil
soil-bio-038.text: When rain falls on dry soil, its respiration usually bursts to a very high level, then declines as the soil dries. This is the Birch effect, the influence of soil moisture on the cycling of carbon in soil. Sudden wetting can burst bacterial cells. Their released contents feed other bacteria and briefly boost {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. Through repeated drying and rewetting, microbial communities shift in diversity and composition.

soil-bio-050.title: Biofilms, the slime cities where soil bacteria live
soil-bio-050.text: In soil and on plant surfaces, most bacteria live bound in biofilms, nicknamed cities for microbes. A biofilm is a community of microorganisms whose cells stick to each other, and often to a surface, inside a self-made slime described in {{ref:soil-bio-080}}. The slime mixes polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and DNA, and can hold many times its dry weight in water. It shelters residents, lets them share nutrients and keeps enzymes close as an external digestion system. Soils with more clay minerals hold more bacteria as biofilms on clay surfaces. On roots, biofilms of growth-promoting bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas and Azospirillum can prime a plant's resistance to pathogens. Biofilms help cycle nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and oxygen. Their internal gradients let nitrate-making microbes work near the surface, while oxygen-free microbes deeper inside run {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. In soil, biofilms can clog pores. In sewage works and slow sand filters they are put to work stripping pollutants from water.

soil-bio-080.title: Extracellular polymeric substances, the glue of microbial life
soil-bio-080.text: Between 50% and 90% of the organic material in a biofilm is the slime its microbes secrete. Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) are high-molecular-weight natural polymers that microorganisms release into their surroundings. They are mostly polysaccharides and proteins, with DNA, lipids and humic compounds. They hold biofilms together and protect the microbes inside from harsh conditions, mechanical removal and antimicrobials. Exopolysaccharides help nitrogen-fixing bacteria attach to plant roots and soil particles, so the bacteria can colonize roots and the soil around them. EPS also shape the soil itself. Together with microbial cells they can block soil pores in bioclogging, lowering hydraulic conductivity. They make sediment more stable by changing its cohesion, permeability and erosion, and they affect the precipitation of minerals, especially carbonates. They adsorb metal cations such as copper, lead, nickel and cadmium, which helps clean up heavy metals. EPS from the bacterium Zoogloea and the fungus Aspergillus niger even remove polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from contaminated soils, using enzymes that degrade them.

soil-bio-051.title: Five stages from a lone cell to a biofilm
soil-bio-051.text: A {{ref:soil-bio-050}} grows up in five major stages. It starts with reversible attachment. Free-floating cells settle on a surface, held at first by weak van der Waals forces and hydrophobic effects. In stage two, attachment becomes irreversible as cells anchor with structures such as pili and more cells gather. Stages three and four are maturation, as cell clusters embedded in the matrix grow into micro-colonies. The fifth stage, dispersal, releases cells that go on to colonize new surfaces.

reviews.life-in-the-soil: Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity, from viruses and bacteria to moles and gophers. Its members form a food web in which bacteria and fungi break dead material into simple nutrients, and the bacterial and fungal channels carry most of the flow. Their combined work leaves the soil as soil respiration, about half from roots, and temperature, moisture and nitrogen speed or slow it. Earthworms and other ecosystem engineers remake the soil itself, leaving casts and burrow linings richer in nutrients than the soil around them. Most soil microbes have never been cultured, so DNA read straight from the soil is only now revealing how this living world is organized.
